rigging.cap: Stehendes Gut stützt den Mast. Laufendes Gut dient zum Setzen und Trimmen der Segel.
rigging.source_cap: Standing rigging holds the mast up. Running rigging moves.
rigging.cap_rationale: The German nautical categories distinguish mast support from the rigging used to set and trim sails. Both functions match the drawing's color legend.

texts.rationale: The fixed mast-to-bow support is the Vorstag. The label points to that forward stay.
The permanent masthead-to-stern stay is the Achterstag. Backstag denotes a running backstay and would misidentify this drawing.
These supports brace the mast sideways. Wanten is the nautical plural of Want.
The transverse mast struts spread the shrouds. Salinge is the plural used by the sailing lexicon.
Fall identifies a sail-hoisting line; it is not a sheet or the separate meaning of mast rake.
Schot is the line that adjusts a sail's position. The diagram shows the mainsheet arrangement at the boom.
The UK sailing term kicker here means the boom vang: tackle preventing the boom from rising.
This line supports the main boom from the masthead when the sail does not support it. The sailing lexicons call that line Dirk.
Stehendes Gut is the collective nautical term for stays and shrouds supporting the mast; the legend describes their function.

texts.de: Laufendes Gut: setzt und trimmt Segel
texts.rationale: Laufendes Gut is the movable rigging used to hoist and trim sails. The functional wording is more precise than a literal translation of moves.

sail-parts.cap: Dreieckiges Großsegel. Der Bug ist rechts.
sail-parts.source_cap: Triangular mainsail, with the bow to the right.
sail-parts.cap_rationale: Großsegel names the mainsail and Bug the bow. The right-facing orientation is a fact of this source drawing, confirmed by its mast and forward sail edge.

texts.rationale: The upper sail corner is Kopf. Segelkopf makes the referent explicit and matches the existing course card.
This is the lower forward sail corner, Hals. Tack as a manoeuvre would be Wende, which is wrong for this label.
Schothorn is the lower aft sail corner, opposite the Hals along the Unterliek.
The forward sail edge beside the mast is Vorliek. The noun luff here does not name the manoeuvre anluven.
Achterliek is the aft sail edge from head to clew, on the left because the bow is to the right.
Unterliek names the bottom sail edge, from tack to clew, rather than an anatomical foot.
Mast is the upright spar beside the mainsail; the sailing-school diagram uses this same term.
Baum is the spar attached by one end to the mast. The depicted mainsail boom is also called Großbaum.
